objective.text: Learn the words point, line segment, line, ray and angle. Draw them and find them in shapes.

explanations.title: A point marks a place
explanations.text: A point marks one exact place. We draw a point as a small dot. We name it with a capital letter. A real point has no size at all.

explanations.title: Line segment and line
explanations.text: A line segment has two endpoints. It is a straight path from one point to the other. A line has arrows on both ends. It goes on forever in both directions.

explanations.title: Ray
explanations.text: A ray has one endpoint. It goes on forever in one direction. We say the endpoint letter first. Ray AB starts at point A and goes past point B.

explanations.title: Angle
explanations.text: Two rays with the same endpoint make an angle. We draw a small arc to show the angle. We name it with three letters, like angle ABC.

explanations.title: Segments, rays and lines are related
explanations.text: A segment is a part of a line. Make a segment longer in one direction and you show a ray. Make it longer in both directions and you show a line.

examples.title: Segment AB and line AB
examples.text: Draw points A and B. Join them with a straight edge to make segment AB. Extend it on both ends and add arrows to show line AB.

examples.title: Ray AB, ray AC and angle BAC
examples.text: Ray AB and ray AC both start at point A. They share an endpoint, so they make an angle. We can call it angle BAC.

examples.title: Parts of a rectangle
examples.text: A rectangle has 4 points where segments meet, 4 line segments and 4 angles. Each side is part of a larger ray. We do not have to draw the rays to imagine them.

objective.text: Use a right angle to tell if an angle is equal to, greater than, or less than a right angle. Draw right, acute and obtuse angles.

explanations.title: Make a right angle by folding
explanations.text: Fold a piece of paper in half. Fold it in half again. The corner you make is a right angle. You can use it as a right angle template.

explanations.title: Compare with the template
explanations.text: Line up the corner and one side of the template with the angle. If the other side matches exactly, it is a right angle. If it is outside the template, the angle is greater. If it is inside, the angle is less.

explanations.title: Right, acute and obtuse
explanations.text: A right angle has a small square in its corner. An acute angle is less than a right angle. An obtuse angle is greater than a right angle but less than a straight angle.

explanations.title: Straight angle
explanations.text: Draw a straight line and mark three points on it. The two rays make a special angle. It is called a straight angle. An obtuse angle is smaller than a straight angle.

examples.title: Find the right angles
examples.text: Place the template on each angle. The angles whose sides match the template exactly are right angles. Mark each with a small square in the corner.

examples.title: Draw three kinds of angle
examples.text: Draw one ray. Use the template to draw a second ray that makes a right angle. Then draw an acute angle and an obtuse angle. Show each with an arc.

objective.text: Find, name and draw perpendicular lines. Perpendicular lines cross to make right angles.

explanations.title: What perpendicular means
explanations.text: Two lines are perpendicular when they cross to make right angles. A cross, a plus sign and the letters T and L have perpendicular lines. Check with a right angle template.

examples.title: A pentagon with no perpendicular lines
examples.text: Place the template on the sides of the pentagon. The sides make obtuse angles. They cross but do not make right angles, so there are no perpendicular lines.

explanations.text: Two angles can have different side lengths and still measure the same. The angles match when you put one on top of the other. Each angle is a fraction of 360 degrees. You can extend the sides to make an angle easier to measure.

objective.text: Measure angles with a protractor. Measure angles bigger than 180 degrees. Draw an angle with a given measure.

explanations.title: Line up, then read
explanations.text: Put the center hole of the protractor on the vertex. Line up one side of the angle with the zero line. Read the number where the other side crosses the arc. A circular protractor and a 180 protractor give the same measure.

explanations.title: Angle greater than 180: subtract from 360
explanations.text: A 180 protractor is too small for a big angle. Extend the arc to make a full circle. Measure the smaller angle. The whole turn is 360 degrees. The big angle is 360 minus the smaller angle.

explanations.title: Angle greater than 180: add on to 180
explanations.text: Extend one side of the angle in a straight line. A straight line is 180 degrees. Measure the new small angle. Add 180 and the small angle to find the whole angle.

explanations.title: Draw an angle with a protractor
explanations.text: Draw a ray and label its endpoint. Put the center of the protractor on the endpoint and the ray on the zero line. Mark a small point above the measure you want. Draw a second ray from the endpoint through the mark. Check with the protractor.

examples.title: One angle, two protractors
examples.text: Measure an angle with a circular protractor. It reads 45 degrees. Measure it with a 180 protractor. It also reads 45 degrees.

examples.title: 230 degrees two ways
examples.text: A big angle has another angle of 130 degrees around the same point. 360 minus 130 is 230. Or extend a side to make a 180 degree line and a 50 degree angle. 180 plus 50 is 230.

examples.title: Draw 133 degrees
examples.text: The protractor shows tens. 133 is between 130 and 140. Start at 130 and count the tick marks up: 131, 132, 133. Mark the third tick. Draw the second ray through the mark.

explanations.text: Fold a clock in half. Fold it in half again. This makes fourths. Moving the hour hand from the 12 to the 3 is one fourth of the way around. It is 90 degrees.

explanations.title: Angles around a point make 360
explanations.text: Fit shapes around a central point like puzzle pieces. Their angles add up to 360 degrees, one full turn. Four squares fit, so 90 plus 90 plus 90 plus 90 is 360.

explanations.title: Divide 360 to find one angle
explanations.text: If equal angles fit around a point, divide 360 by the number of angles. Six equal triangle corners fit, so 360 divided by 6 is 60. Each triangle angle is 60 degrees.

explanations.title: Fold to split an angle
explanations.text: Fold a paper to make a straight angle of 180 degrees. Fold it again to make a right angle of 90 degrees. Fold again to split the right angle into two equal angles of 45 degrees. The parts add up to the whole.

explanations.title: The whole is the sum of the parts
explanations.text: When you split an angle into parts, the parts add up to the whole angle. The whole does not change when you fold. If your parts do not add up to the whole, check your measuring.

explanations.title: Find a missing part
explanations.text: Know the whole and one part? Subtract the part from the whole. A right angle is 90 degrees. If one part is 60 degrees, the other part is 90 minus 60.

explanations.title: Use a box for the unknown
explanations.text: Write an equation with a box for the unknown angle. Start with the known part: 132 plus a box equals 180. Or start with the whole: 180 minus 132 equals the box.

explanations.title: Three parts
explanations.text: A straight angle can be split into three parts. Add the two parts you know. Subtract that sum from 180 to find the third part.

examples.title: Four 45 degree angles
examples.text: A straight angle is split into four equal angles. 45 plus 45 plus 45 plus 45 is 180. Three of them make 45 plus 45 plus 45, which is 135.

examples.title: Right angle with a 60 degree part
examples.text: A right angle is 90 degrees. One part is 60 degrees. The other part is 90 minus 60, which is 30 degrees.

examples.title: Straight angle with a 132 degree part
examples.text: A straight angle is 180 degrees. One part is 132 degrees. 132 plus a box equals 180. 180 minus 132 is 48, so the box is 48.

examples.title: Straight angle with parts 45, 30 and a box
examples.text: 45 plus 30 plus a box equals 180. 45 plus 30 is 75. 180 minus 75 is 105. The unknown angle is 105 degrees.

objective.text: Find unknown angles around a point and on crossing lines. Angles around a point add to 360 degrees.

explanations.title: Angles around a point add to 360
explanations.text: A full turn around a point is 360 degrees. Add the angles you know. Subtract that sum from 360. The answer is the unknown angle. It works for any number of parts.

explanations.title: Two crossing lines
explanations.text: When two lines cross, they make four angles. Angles across from each other are equal. Two angles side by side on one line add up to 180 degrees.

objective.text: Find lines of symmetry in shapes. A line of symmetry is a fold line where both halves match exactly.

explanations.title: Fold and match
explanations.text: Fold a shape so that both sides match exactly. The fold line is a line of symmetry. A shape can have one line, more than one line, or none.

explanations.title: Count the lines in familiar shapes
explanations.text: A square has 4 lines of symmetry. A rectangle that is not a square has 2. A rhombus has 2. A parallelogram has none. The trapezoid in class has 1.

explanations.title: A circle has infinite lines
explanations.text: Every point on a circle is the same distance from the center. Any fold through the center makes two matching halves. So a circle has an infinite number of lines of symmetry.

explanations.title: Complete a figure with a mirror image
explanations.text: A dashed line shows a line of symmetry. Draw the mirror image of the half on the other side. On a grid, count squares. A half that is 4 units wide makes a whole figure that is 8 units wide.

examples.title: Square: 4 folds
examples.text: Fold a square in half side to side, top to bottom and along each diagonal. The halves match each time. A square has 4 lines of symmetry.

examples.title: Rectangle: 2 folds
examples.text: Fold a rectangle in half across its length and across its width. The halves match. A diagonal fold does not match. A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry.

examples.title: A hand has no line of symmetry
examples.text: The five fingers of a hand are all different. The thumb and the pinky do not match. Folding top to bottom does not match either. So a hand has no line of symmetry.

objective.text: Sort triangles by side length and by angle size. Use the names equilateral, isosceles, scalene, acute, right and obtuse.

explanations.title: Classify by side length
explanations.text: An equilateral triangle has all 3 sides equal. An isosceles triangle has at least 2 sides equal. A scalene triangle has no sides equal. We draw a tick mark on sides that are equal.

explanations.title: Classify by angle size
explanations.text: A triangle with one right angle is a right triangle. A triangle with one obtuse angle is an obtuse triangle. A triangle with only acute angles is an acute triangle. A small square marks a right angle.

explanations.title: Fold to see equal sides and angles
explanations.text: Fold an isosceles triangle on its line of symmetry. The two sides that meet are equal. The two angles that meet are equal too. An equilateral triangle has 3 lines of symmetry and 3 equal angles.

explanations.title: The other two angles of a right triangle
explanations.text: Fold the two smaller angles of a right triangle into the right angle. They fit exactly. So the other two angles add up to 90 degrees.

explanations.title: What is a triangle?
explanations.text: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 angles. It is made from 3 points that are not in a line, joined by 3 segments. If all 3 points lie on one line, there is no triangle.

examples.title: Triangles A to F
examples.text: Triangle A has 3 equal sides and only acute angles. B has 2 equal sides and only acute angles. C has 3 different sides and an obtuse angle. D has 3 different sides and a right angle. E has 2 equal sides and a right angle. F has 2 equal sides and an obtuse angle.

examples.title: Equilateral is a special isosceles
examples.text: An isosceles triangle has at least 2 equal sides and 2 equal angles. An equilateral triangle has those too, but it has 3 equal sides and 3 equal angles.

objective.text: Draw triangles that match two clues, like obtuse and isosceles. Decide which clue pairs can and cannot go together.

explanations.title: Every triangle has at least two names
explanations.text: Each triangle can be named by its sides and by its angles. A triangle might be right and isosceles. An equilateral triangle has three names: equilateral, isosceles and acute.

explanations.title: Build an obtuse isosceles triangle
explanations.text: Use a protractor to draw an angle bigger than 90 degrees, such as 100. Draw two sides of the same length next to it, such as 2 inches each. Join the ends. Measure to check: one obtuse angle and two equal sides.

explanations.title: Build a right scalene triangle
explanations.text: Draw the right angle first. Then draw two sides of different lengths. Join the ends. Measure to check that there is a 90 degree angle and all three sides differ.

explanations.title: Which clue pairs can exist?
explanations.text: A triangle cannot be both scalene and equilateral. An equilateral triangle cannot be obtuse or right because its three angles are acute and equal. A scalene acute triangle can exist. An equilateral triangle is also isosceles.

examples.title: Right scalene
examples.text: Draw a 90 degree angle first. Draw two sides of different lengths. Join the ends. The triangle is right because of the 90 degree angle. It is scalene because no sides match.

examples.title: Scalene acute exists
examples.text: A triangle can have three different side lengths and three acute angles. It is both scalene and acute.

objective.text: Use attributes to build quadrilaterals on triangular and square grid paper. Name each one as a rhombus, parallelogram, rectangle, trapezoid or square.

explanations.title: Rhombus: a parallelogram with four equal sides
explanations.text: A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides. Its angles do not have to be right angles.

explanations.title: Two triangles that share a side make a rhombus
explanations.text: On triangular grid paper, every small triangle is equilateral. Shade two that share a side. The shape has four equal sides and two pairs of parallel sides.

explanations.title: Angles of a grid rhombus
explanations.text: The two acute angles are equal because they are angles of equilateral triangles. The two obtuse angles are equal because each is two of those angles together.

explanations.title: Build a rectangle on a triangular grid
explanations.text: Trace a pair of parallel lines. Draw two segments perpendicular to them. Check with a ruler and right angle template, then mark the right angles.

explanations.title: Build a parallelogram with no right angles
explanations.text: On a square grid, trace two parallel segments of equal length. Join their ends with a third segment that is not on a gridline. Draw the fourth segment parallel to the third.

explanations.title: Build a trapezoid with only one pair of parallel sides
explanations.text: Start with a parallelogram. Change the third and fourth segments so they are not parallel. Now only one pair of sides is parallel.
